entities.name: Board for Advance Rulings (Income Tax)
entities.statutory_basis: Income Tax Act 1961, Chapter XIX-B (ss.245N–245V) as substituted by Finance Act 2021 s.98 — reconstituted as 'Board for Advance Rulings' from 'Authority for Advance Rulings'. Two Boards constituted with retired ITAT Presidents/Vice Presidents. Original AAR (single-member, retired SC Judge as Chairman) abolished by Finance Act 2021 w.e.f. 01.04.2021.
entities.data_quality_notes: Independence concern: Finance Act 2021 reconstitution replaced retired SC Judge Chairman with senior IRS officers — structural shift from judicial to departmental composition. Contested by taxpayer bar (pending writ petitions in several HCs challenging constitutionality of non-judicial composition for advance rulings).   Two Boards at Delhi and Mumbai constituted by CBDT Notification No. 96/2021 (S.O. 3561(E)) dated 1 September 2021 — corrected from prior erroneous reference to 92/2021 (drt_b4). Rulings binding on applicant and CBDT (s.245S) but subject to writ jurisdiction of HC under Art.226/227. No appeal to ITAT or HC as of right. created_year reflects original AAR (Finance Act 1993 Chapter XIX-B); reconstitution year 2021. v1.2 judge_strength stub attached

entities.name: Assessing Officer (Income Tax) — Generic
entities.statutory_basis: Income Tax Act 1961 s.2(7A) (definition of Assessing Officer); ss.120–133C (jurisdiction, powers, and functions of income-tax authorities including AOs); ss.143–144 (assessment procedure); ss.147–148A (reassessment); s.156 (demand notice). Appeals against AO orders lie to CIT(A)/JCIT(A) under s.246A, thence to ITAT under s.253.
entities.data_quality_notes:
Generic entity representing the Assessing Officer cadre across all Income Tax field formations. AO is the originating authority in the IT appellate chain: AO → CIT(A) → ITAT → HC → SC.
This entity models the structural role, not any individual AO or charge/ward. Actual formations are allocated by CBDT through charge orders; individual AO jurisdictions assigned under IT Act 1961 s.120 via CBDT notification.
No judge_strength or case_volume fields applicable — volume statistics are reported at CBDT/department level, not per AO unit.

entities.name: Board of Revenue (Generic)
entities.statutory_basis: Constituted under state-specific Board of Revenue Acts or Revenue Codes. Principal examples: Board of Revenue Act (Uttar Pradesh) 1922 (as amended); Rajasthan Board of Revenue Act 1949; Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code 1954 (Part II); Tamil Nadu Board of Revenue Abolition Act 1980 (abolished in TN — see structural_variations). Exercises highest revisional/appellate jurisdiction over revenue/land records, land acquisition compensation, and tenancy matters within the state.
entities.data_quality_notes: Generic node. Boards of Revenue are quasi-judicial state bodies sitting atop the revenue courts hierarchy (Tehsildar → SDO → Collector → Commissioner → Board of Revenue). Not all states retain a Board of Revenue; Tamil Nadu abolished it (1980), Karnataka merged functions into Revenue Appellate Tribunal, and some NE states never had one. Appeals from BoR orders lie to the respective HC. created_year 1951 is approximate (many BoRs predate Independence; reconstituted under post-1950 state statutes). ministry_responsible left null — state Revenue or Land Records Department is the administrative parent; no universal entity_id mapped in graph yet. v1.2 judge_strength stub attached. entities.name: Court Martial (Generic — Army/Navy/Air Force)
entities.statutory_basis: Army Act 1950 (Chapters VI–IX); Navy Act 1957 (Chapter VIII); Air Force Act 1950 (Chapter VI); Armed Forces Tribunal Act 2007 (established AFT as external appellate body post-2007).
entities.data_quality_notes: Generic stub covering GCM, SGCM, DCM, SCM convened under all three service Acts. Key structural gap: Summary Court Martial (SCM) has no right of appeal to AFT — the accused's sole remedy is post-conviction petition to Chief of Army Staff / Central Government under Army Act 1950 § 164. This is a significant accountability lacuna. Pre-AFT (before 2009 operationalisation), no external judicial body existed; High Courts exercised writ jurisdiction only. Appellate path (post-2007): finding/sentence → Confirming Authority → AFT (for GCM/DCM/SGCM). SCM sentences not appealable to AFT (AFT Act 2007 § 15 read with Army Act § 164). Appointment of court martial members: Convening Officer (generally a senior officer) convenes and nominates members; Judge Advocate (a JAG-branch officer) is appointed to advise on law. No civilian element in composition. No public docket or cause list; proceedings not published. judge_strength not modelled — court martial is an ad-hoc body, not a permanent court with sanctioned judicial posts. v1.2 judge_strength stub attached

entities.name: Dispute Resolution Panel (Income Tax)
entities.statutory_basis: Income Tax Act 1961, s.144C as inserted by Finance (No.2) Act 2009 s.42. DRP is a collegium of three Principal Commissioners / Commissioners of Income Tax designated by CBDT. Not a separate statutory tribunal — constituted as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism within CBDT for eligible assesses (primarily foreign companies and transfer-pricing cases).
entities.data_quality_notes: Independence circularity concern: DRP members are CBDT officers adjudicating objections to draft assessment orders passed by CBDT officers. Directions issued by DRP under s.144C(5) are binding on the Assessing Officer but do not preclude ITAT appeal (s.144C(10) — assessee may appeal to ITAT against final order; department may not). DRP is NOT a tribunal distinct from CBDT — it is an internal collegium. Classifying as RegulatoryBodyQJ in regulatory_bodies cluster to reflect quasi-judicial function within the executive; type CentralTribunal would mischaracterise independence. DRP panels constituted at major cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Ahmedabad) per CBDT notifications. No public annual report. Pendency data not publicly disaggregated from ITAT inflows.

entities.statutory_basis: Employees' Provident Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act 1952, ss.5A–5AA (Central Board of Trustees), ss.5D–5E (Central Provident Fund Commissioner). EPFO exercises quasi-judicial functions through its officers under ss.7A (determination of EPF dues — Enquiry Officers), 7B (review), 14B (imposition of damages). These officer-level adjudicative orders are appealable to EPFAT. EPFO itself is a statutory executive body; only its adjudicatory officers have quasi-judicial character.
entities.data_quality_notes: EPFO is classified ExecutiveBody (not CentralTribunal) because it is primarily an executive/statutory fund management body. EPFO administers EPF, EPS (Employees' Pension Scheme 1995), and EDLI (Employees' Deposit Linked Insurance Scheme 1976). Manages ~280 million subscriber accounts (as of 2024 EPFO annual report); collects ~INR 1.8 lakh crore annually. Social Security Code 2020 will reconstitute governance structure when notified.

entities.statutory_basis: Insurance Act 1938 § 114A (rule-making power); Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017 (GSR 877(E), notified 11 September 2017, in force; superseded 1998 Rules). Constituted by Council for Insurance Ombudsmen (Governing Body of Insurance Council — GBIC).
entities.data_quality_notes:
Official institutional name under Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017 is 'Insurance Ombudsman' (not an appellate tribunal). The _generic suffix applies: 17 regional ombudsman centres operate under a common statutory scheme; this entity models the generic pattern (cf. state_election_commission_generic, court_martial_generic). Two-tier model:
  Layer 1 — Insurance Ombudsman (17 offices): consumer-facing mediation and
  binding award up to Rs 50 lakh (G.S.R. amendment notified 10 Nov 2023; prior cap
  Rs 30 lakh under 2017 Rules as amended 2021).
  Layer 2 — Securities Appellate Tribunal (SAT): appellate body for IRDAI
  regulatory orders under Insurance Laws (Amendment) Act 2015 § 110C.
Awards binding on insurer once complainant accepts (Insurance Ombudsman Rules 2017 r.17). No direct contempt power — if insurer defies, complainant escalates to IRDAI or consumer court. Draft IRDAI IIO Guidelines 2025 propose stronger enforcement. This entity models Layer 1. SAT and IRDAI are modelled separately in repo. Former draft id insurance_appellate_generic was incorrect — renamed 2026-06-12.

Four Labour Codes (2019-2020) enacted but rules not yet fully notified as of August 2025.
entities.data_quality_notes: Expanded from C08 stub (drt_b3). HQ: Rafi Marg, New Delhi. Budget figure ₹13,221.73 crore from Wikipedia citing 2023-24 estimate. Key subordinate bodies: EPFO (autonomous), ESIC (autonomous), CGIT-cum-LCs (22 seats), Central Board for Workers' Education (CBWE), Director General of Employment, Director General of Labour Welfare, Chief Labour Commissioner (Central). Four Labour Codes enacted 2019-2020 consolidate 29 central laws — full implementation pending as of August 2025 (rules gazette not complete for all states). Skill development functions transferred to Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship in 2014.

entities.statutory_basis: Press Council Act 1978 (§ 4 — establishment; § 14 — quasi-judicial powers)
entities.data_quality_notes: Press Council Act 1978 repealed and replaced the Press Council Act 1965 which had established the first PCI in 1966; re-established under 1978 Act. Quasi-judicial function: PCI can censure a newspaper/news agency/editor or journalist but has no punitive power beyond censure — it cannot impose fines or criminal penalties (§ 14). Appellate path: PCI censure order → challenge by writ petition to High Court. Structural gap: PCI's jurisdiction covers only print media; digital/online news portals and TV news channels are outside its statutory remit as of 2026 (pending Press and Registration of Periodicals Act 2023 implementation, which modernises registration but does not expand quasi-judicial scope to digital media). The PRP Act 2023 (in force) supersedes PRB Act 1867 for registration but does not dissolve or restructure PCI.

jurisdiction_types: Superintendence, direction and control of elections to Panchayats and Municipalities
Election dispute quasi-judicial functions (where state law provides)

entities.constitutional_basis: Article 243K (Panchayats) and Article 243ZA (Municipalities) — inserted by Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act 1992 and Constitution (74th Amendment) Act 1992, both in force from 24 April 1993.
entities.statutory_basis: State Election Commission Act / Rules enacted by each state legislature; varies by state. Generic pattern: State Commissioner appointed by Governor, removal procedure mirrors Election Commission of India (requires SC reference per Art. 243K(2)).
entities.data_quality_notes:
This is a generic stub covering the common constitutional pattern for all 28 States and 3 UTs with legislatures (J&K, Puducherry, Delhi). Key variations across states:
  — Some states have merged SEC with general election administration (not best practice).
  — Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh SECs have faced litigation over non-constitution of
    panchayat bodies for extended periods.
  — J&K SEC reconstituted after J&K Reorganisation Act 2019.
Appellate path for election disputes: The bar on civil court jurisdiction (Arts. 243O, 243ZG) means election disputes go to state-constituted Election Tribunals → High Court (second appeal / writ) → Supreme Court (SLP). State-specific SEC entities (e.g. sec_maharashtra) should be modelled as separate entities with state_data fields when state packs are created. judge_strength not applicable (SEC is a single-member body by constitutional design).

entities.name: State Industrial Tribunal (Generic)
entities.statutory_basis: Industrial Disputes Act 1947, s.7A (Industrial Tribunals). State Governments constitute State Industrial Tribunals to adjudicate matters in the Second and Third Schedules of the Act (Third Schedule includes wages, hours, bonus, profit- sharing, retrenchment, closure). State Industrial Tribunals have wider jurisdiction than Labour Courts. Distinction from CGIT (s.7A): State-sphere industries are referred to State Industrial Tribunals; Central-sphere industries to CGIT. Industrial Relations Code 2020 (enacted; not yet operative as of June 2026).
entities.data_quality_notes: Generic node for State Industrial Tribunals (state sphere) constituted under IDA 1947 s.7A. Distinction from cgit_* nodes: these handle State Government references for state-sphere industries (industries not in the Central sphere list per IDA s.2(a) read with Ministry of Labour orders). Appeals from State IT awards lie to respective HC under Art. 226/227; no statutory appeal route. Awards enforceable as Civil Court decrees (s.17A). Industrial Relations Code 2020 will replace this structure when notified. Count: 20–30 benches nationally; exact figure not centrally published. ministry_responsible left null — each state's Labour Department. v1.2 judge_strength stub attached. entities.statutory_basis: Trade Marks Act 1999 §§ 6–9 (Registry and Registrar); Trade Marks Rules 2017.
entities.data_quality_notes: created_year: 1940 — Trade Marks Registry established under Trade Marks Act 1940 (original establishment). Current operative statute is Trade Marks Act 1999 (§§ 6–9); use 1999 only if modelling the current Act regime rather than registry lineage. statutory_basis field reflects the 1999 Act. Trade Marks Registry head office: Mumbai. Branch offices: Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai, Ahmedabad. The Registry is subordinate to CGPDTM (patent_controller entity in JEM). Quasi-judicial function: Registrar hears trade mark opposition (§ 21) and rectification proceedings (§ 57); these are appealable to HC post-IPAB abolition. Pre-2021 appellate path: Registrar → IPAB → HC → SC. Post-2021 appellate path: Registrar → High Court (§ 91, as amended by Tribunal Reforms Act 2021) → Division Bench → SC. Relationship to patent_controller: trade_marks_registry is a sub-office under CGPDTM; suggest AdministrativeSupervision edge trade_marks_registry → patent_controller for maintainer wiring.

The direct PDF (Annual_Report_06012026.pdf) independently passes liveness. [maintainer downgrade] statutorily_required was recorded as 'yes' on https://lawgist.in/telecom-regulatory-authority-of-india-act/24, a private reproduction of the Act rather than a primary provision. NJDG snapshot case_volume merged complaint_mechanism populated from SC In-House Procedure 1999 and SC Stay Order Feb 2025 (suo moto). criminal_prosecution.requires_sanction_from set to governor_state per Veeraswami (1991) for HC judges. lokpal_jurisdiction No per operative Feb 2025 stay; revisit if SC decides finally. audit.conduct_oversight_body set to in_house_procedure_sc (same procedure governs HC judges).

appointment.tenure: Until age 62 (Article 217)

bias_complaint_to.mechanism: In-House Procedure (SC Resolution 1999, extended to HC judges). Complaint lodged with the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court; if the allegation is against that Chief Justice, complaint filed directly with the CJI. CJI may constitute a 3-judge in-house committee to inquire. Report is confidential. Complainant has no locus in inquiry proceedings.

complaint_mechanism.removal_mechanism: Address by Parliament — Article 217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4). Motion by 100+ LS MPs or 50+ RS MPs. No HC judge has been successfully removed in Indian history.
complaint_mechanism.lokpal_jurisdiction_note: SC stayed Lokpal's attempt to assert jurisdiction over HC judges (suo moto, Feb 2025). Lokpal had separately ruled in Jan 2025 that it cannot hear complaints against SC judges (Art 124 basis); the Feb 2025 stay extends the same bar to HC judges. Status: active litigation, but operative bar currently in place.
complaint_mechanism.source: K. Veeraswami v Union of India (1991) 3 SCC 655; SC In-House Procedure 1999; SC Stay Order Feb 2025 (suo moto re HC judges)

entities.data_quality_notes: One of three dedicated Commercial Courts at the District Judge level constituted at Kancheepuram at Chengalpattu by Notification No. II(2)/HO/887/2021 under s.3(1), Commercial Courts Act 2015, after consultation with the High Court, Madras. The same notification batch designates this court as the Commercial Appellate Court for its district (Notification No. II(2)/HO/888/2021, s.3A), so no separate tn_commercial_appellate_court_* entity is emitted — the appellate forum is this same court. A predecessor commercial court existed here from 2016 under the class-wide designation in Notification No. II(2)/HO/417/2016, superseded in 2021. Structural-first entry: no case_volume, no judge_strength.

entities.name: Chief Judicial Magistrate Court, The Nilgiris at Udhagamandalam
aliases: Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, The Nilgiris at Uthagamandalam
Chief Judicial Magistrate, The Nilgiris District at Udhagamandalam
entities.data_quality_notes:
ESTABLISHMENT. Established by Home Department notification No. II(2)/HO/141/2024 [G.O. Ms. No. 130, Home (Courts-III), 9th February 2024], published in the Tamil Nadu Government Gazette No. 10, Part II-Section 2, 6 March 2024, at p.72. The gazette heading reads "Constitution of a Seperate Chief Judicial Magistrate Court at Udhagamandalam in the Nilgiris District under the code of Code of Criminal Procedure"; the operative text reads "In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (1) of Section 11 of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Central Act 2 of 1974), the Governor of Tamil Nadu, after consultation with the High Court, Madras hereby establishes a Court of Judicaial [sic] Magistrate at Udhagamandalam in the Nilgiris District." created_year 2024 is taken from the gazette publication date (2024-03-06); the underlying G.O. is dated 2024-02-09.
CJM CHARACTER — CORROBORATED BY TWO FURTHER PRIMARIES. (i) Judicial notification No. VI(1)/514/2023 (Roc. No. 25374/2020/G/Judn), TNGG No. 33, Part VI-Section 1, 16 August 2023, pp.326-329, issued by the District Court-cum-Chief Judicial Magistrate, Udhagamandalam under CrPC s.14(1), names "Chief Judicial Magistrate, The Nilgiris District at Udhagamandalam (Proposed Court)" and allots it, inter alia, "All cases relating to the offences which are triable by the Chief Judicial Magistrate alone", with effect from the date the CJM assumes charge. (ii) Notification No. II(2)/HO/656/2026 [G.O. Ms. No. 238, Home (Transport-IV), 24 July 2026], TNGG No. 34, Part II-Section 2, 26 August 2026, amends the MACT notification to replace "Court of District Judge-cum-Chief Judicial Magistrate, The Nilgris at Uthagamandalam" with "Court of District judge, The Nilgiris at Uthagamandalam" and to insert a separate entry "(aa) Court of Chief Judicial Magistrate, The Nilgiris at Uthagamandalam" with presiding officer "Chief Judicial Magistrate, The Nilgiris at Uthagamandalam". operational_status Active rests on that 2026 instrument, which treats the court as constituted and presided over.
SENTENCING CEILING (criminal quantum; not pecuniary). BNSS 2023 s.23(1), verbatim: "The Court of a Chief Judicial Magistrate may pass any sentence authorised by law except a sentence of death or of imprisonment for life or of imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years." Sourced from the enacted Act text (Gazette of India Extraordinary Part II-Section 1 No. 54, 25 December 2023, Act No. 46 of 2023) at the MHA-hosted URL below, p.10 of the PDF.
NOT SOURCED / DELIBERATELY ABSENT. Transliteration in TN primaries varies ("Udhagamandalam" / "Uthagamandalam"; "Nilgiris" / "Nilgris"). The exact date on which the Chief Judicial Magistrate assumed charge was not found in any document opened for this run. No case_volume or judge_strength (structural-first track). A structured criminal-jurisdiction block keyed to offence gravity is deferred to the detail phase.

entities.name: Arbitration Council of India
entities.statutory_basis: Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act 2019, Part IA, Sections 43A–43M (inserted into Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996).
entities.data_quality_notes: ACI not constituted as of June 2026 — ~7 years since 2019 amendment legislation. SC issued notice to Union government 23 January 2025 to explain prolonged delay. GoI press release (Feb 2026) confirms non-constitution. Draft Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill 2024 proposes revised powers; Bill in public consultation.

sources.label: Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act 2019 — Part IA
SC notice to Union on ACI constitution — The Hindu, 23 Jan 2025
Draft Arbitration Bill 2024 — Ministry of Law & Justice

appointment.tenure: 3 years or age 70 (whichever earlier); non-renewable

complaint_mechanism.removal_mechanism: Central Government, on recommendation of committee. Chairperson removable only on grounds stated in statute.
complaint_mechanism.lokpal_jurisdiction_note: Body not constituted — question does not arise.
complaint_mechanism.source: Arbitration and Conciliation Act 1996, Section 43F (as amended 2019)

structural_variations.description: Draft Arbitration Bill 2024 proposes to replace ACI's grading power with recognition of arbitral institutions and model rules. This would change the composition and functions defined in the 2019 Act if passed.
structural_variations.source: Draft Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill 2024 — Ministry of Law & Justice
structural_variations.independence_risk_note: ACI Chairperson appointed by Central Government in consultation with CJI. CJI consultation is binding. However, Government retains formal appointment power.

gaps.gap_description: Not constituted — ~7 years since 2019 amendment legislation. SC issued notice to Union government 23 January 2025.
gaps.gap_source: Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Act 2019; SC notice Jan 2025

sources.label: Rajya Sabha reply — Mediation Council not yet constituted — PTI, 20 Mar 2025

complaint_mechanism.lokpal_jurisdiction_note: Body not constituted — question does not arise.
complaint_mechanism.source: Mediation Act 2023

gaps.gap_description: Not constituted — ~3 years since Mediation Act 2023 enactment (September 2023). Same legislative vacuum pattern as ACI.

entities.name: Supreme Court of India
entities.data_quality_notes: NJDG snapshot case_volume merged

sources.label: Supreme Court of India — Official Website

appointment.tenure: Until age 65 (Article 124(2))

bias_complaint_to.mechanism: In-House Procedure (SC Resolution 1999). Complaint to CJI. CJI constitutes 3-judge committee. Report is confidential. Complainant has no locus in inquiry proceedings.

complaint_mechanism.removal_mechanism: Impeachment — Article 124(4). Motion by 100+ LS MPs or 50+ RS MPs. Never successfully completed in Indian history.
complaint_mechanism.lokpal_jurisdiction_note: Lokpal ruled in Jan 2025 that it cannot hear complaints against SC judges because the SC is established by Article 124 (Constitution), not an Act of Parliament. SC stayed Lokpal's attempt to assert jurisdiction over HC judges (suo moto, Feb 2025). Status: active litigation.
complaint_mechanism.source: K. Veeraswami v Union of India (1991) 3 SCC 655; SC In-House Procedure 1999; SC Stay Order Feb 2025 (suo moto)

digital_infrastructure.integration_notes: NJDG-SC portal launched in 2023 as part of eCourts Phase III. SC data was the last to be integrated into national NJDG.

judge_strength.notes: Sanctioned/working/vacancy from row A; no Pmt/Addl split shown for SC

entities.name: e-Committee of the Supreme Court of India
entities.statutory_basis: Constituted by Government of India in pursuance of proposal from Chief Justice of India. No separate statutory basis — functions under the administrative authority of the SC and DoJ MMP framework.

appointment.tenure: At pleasure of CJI — no fixed tenure

complaint_mechanism.source: Not applicable — e-Committee is policy/oversight body, not adjudicatory

digital_infrastructure.integration_notes: e-Committee sets standards; NIC (under MeitY) builds and maintains. High Courts are Implementing Agencies under their respective jurisdictions. The Central Project Coordinator (CPC) in each HC is accountable to the e-Committee via the PPMS portal (ecourts.nic.in).

structural_variations.description: The e-Committee is chaired by a sitting SC judge (CJI-designated), making it a judicial body. However, eCourts Mission Mode Project is monitored and funded by Department of Justice, Ministry of Law & Justice (executive). This creates a dual-principal problem: e-Committee sets technology policy; DoJ controls the budget. Every technology decision of scale requires DoJ sanction. No formal dispute resolution mechanism exists between the two bodies for technology disagreements.
structural_variations.source: ecommitteesci.gov.in; doj.gov.in/division/ecourts/
structural_variations.independence_risk_note: The executive (DoJ/MeitY) controls the budget and the technical vendor (NIC). The SC (via e-Committee) controls the policy. This structural tension means the judiciary's technology backbone is ultimately dependent on executive goodwill and budget allocation cycles. No SLA or contractual obligation exists between NIC and the courts.

structural_variations.description: Several HCs have developed custom Case Management Systems that do not fully conform to NIC CIS standards: Bombay HC (custom CMS), Delhi HC (enhanced digital services), Madras HC (independent IT development). relationships.constitutional_basis: Article 124(2) — as interpreted by SC in Second Judges Case (1993) and Third Judges Case (1998)
relationships.notes: The Collegium system is entirely judge-made — not written in the Constitution. Article 124(2) says President appoints "in consultation with" CJI and other judges. SC in Second Judges Case (1993) held this consultation is binding; CJI's recommendation is determinative. This reversed SP Gupta (1981) which had held executive supremacy. The 99th Amendment NJAC (2014) attempted to change this but was struck down in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v Union of India (2015).

sources.label: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v Union of India (1993) 4 SCC 441

relationships.notes: Formal instrument of appointment issued by President. In practice, President acts on Collegium's recommendation. Post-1993, President cannot appoint a judge the Collegium has not recommended.

NJAC was constituted by 99th Constitutional Amendment. Would have replaced the Collegium with a 6-member commission including CJI, 2 senior SC judges, Law Minister, and 2 eminent persons. Struck down by SC 5-judge bench in Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v Union of India (2015) as violating the basic structure of judicial independence. This relationship is HISTORICAL — rendered as faded/ghosted in the UI when time slider is set after 2015.

sources.label: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record v Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1

relationships.constitutional_basis: Article 217(1) — as interpreted by SC Third Judges Case (1998)
relationships.notes: For HC judge appointment, the recommending Collegium involves: CJI + 2 most senior SC judges + HC Chief Justice + most senior HC judge elevated to SC. Governor and State Government consulted but their consultation is advisory only — not binding on the Collegium.

Governor (acting on advice of State Council of Ministers under Art. 163) is consulted on HC judge appointments. This consultation is NOT binding. This is the primary formal channel for state government input into HC appointments — but its non-binding nature means a state government cannot veto an appointment the Collegium has recommended.

Governor appoints, posts and promotes District Judges in consultation with the High Court. HC's consultation is binding (K. Ashok Reddy 1994). For direct recruitment from bar: Governor acts; HC dominates. For promotions from lower service: Governor acts on HC recommendation.
HC consultation on District Judge appointment is binding on the Governor. K. Ashok Reddy v Government of India (1994) SC confirmed HC primacy.
